"The Way has transgressions and non-transgressions. Now you say, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much.
What principle have you seen? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Ji then struck Daoyu three times under the ribs. Daoyu pushed him away and said:
"Your teacher Huangbo has nothing to do with my affairs. When Linji returned to Huangbo, Huangbo saw him coming and said, "This fellow comes and goes;

when will there ever be an end to it? Linji said, "It is precisely because of his grandmotherly concern. He then recounted the previous conversation. Huangbo said, "That old fellow Dayu is too talkative.
How could you have gotten him to come here? Linji said, "Why would I want him to come?"
Huangbo said, "Wait for him to come, and I will give him a thorough beating. Ji said, "What do you mean by 'waiting for him to come'?
He shall eat [the consequences] right now! He immediately slapped him. Huangbo said, "This wind-crazed fellow has come here to pull at a tiger's whiskers. Ji then shouted.
Huangbo said, "Attendant, lead this wind-crazed fellow away to attend to the hall duties. Later, Guishan asked Yangshan, "Regarding Linji..."
He gained the power of Dayu and gained the power of Huangbo. Yangshan said, "Not only can he ride on the tiger's head, he also knows how to seize the tiger's tail.
The Monk of Yanguan asked the Dharma Master, "What sutras and treatises do you master? He replied, "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra. [The Master] said, "In the Avataṃsaka Sūtra..."
“How many kinds of *dharmadhātu* are there? The Master said, “Briefly stated, there are four; explained extensively, they are infinitely layered.
Yanguan held up his whisk and asked, “In which of these kinds of *dharmadhātu* is this included? The Master remained silent for a long while.
Yanguan said, “To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation is the livelihood of ghosts. A solitary lamp beneath the sun—truly, its light is lost.”
[The text] moves down. Miaoxi said: "These two sections are different; they are subsumed under the preceding category.
Master Damei addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, each must turn your minds back to realize the fundamental source; do not pursue its..."
As for the branches: if one attains the root, the branches will arrive of their own accord. If one wishes to recognize the root, one need only understand one's own mind.
This mind is fundamentally the root of all mundane and supramundane phenomena. Therefore, when the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease.
Furthermore, the mind does not arise in dependence upon any good or evil; the myriad phenomena are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).
A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "Mulberry blossoms and willow catkins; bamboo needles and hemp thread.

Master Wuzu Yan addressed the assembly, saying: "Every day since rising, I have leaned upon Linji’s staff, blown the Yunmen flute, responded to Zhaozhou’s clapping, carried Yangshan’s spade, drove Baizhang’s ox, and plowed the fields of Baiyun for seven or eight years."
Gradually, we have established a household. I further appeal to you all: let each person extend a hand to support one another and sing the "Joy of Returning to the Fields.
Pass the time with coarse soup and plain rice. Why? Simply because I wish for the silkworms and wheat to ripen this year.
Rāhula’s son was given one coin. A monk asked Niu-t’ou, “How was it before you had seen the Fourth Patriarch?
He replied, “A heavy burden atop his head. The monk asked, “And after he had seen him? He replied, “A blue cloth covering his front.

The monk asked, “Why did the hundred birds bring flowers to offer him before he had seen the Fourth Patriarch? He replied, “Wealth and honor are what all people desire. The monk asked, “And after he had seen him? He replied, [“...”].
"Why do the hundred birds not bring flowers as offerings? He replied, "Poverty and low status are what people detest.

When Master Guling was traveling on pilgrimage, he attained enlightenment under Baizhang. Upon returning to Dazhong Temple in Fuzhou, his preceptor asked him, "While you were away from me, what accomplishments have you gained?
He replied, "I have no accomplishments at all," whereupon the master sent him to perform manual labor.
One day, while bathing, he commanded his spirit to remove the impurities from his back. The spirit then tapped him on the back and said, "The Buddha hall is magnificent, yet the Buddha is not holy.
His master turned his head to look at him, and the spirit said, "Though the Buddha is not holy, he is nevertheless able to emit light.
On another day, as the master was reading a sutra by the window, a bee flew against the paper of the screen, seeking an exit. Seeing this, the spirit said:
"The world is this vast, yet you refuse to leave it. You merely pore over the old papers of others; when will you ever get anywhere?
His teacher set aside the scriptures and asked, "Whom have you encountered during your travels? I have observed that your speech has been extraordinary from the beginning.
Ling replied, "I have received a place of rest pointed out by Master Baizhang; I now wish to repay his compassionate virtue. Thereupon, his teacher—
"Please preach the Dharma for me. Ling then proclaimed the tradition of Baizhang, saying: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.
Its essence reveals true permanence, unbound by words and letters. The nature of mind is undefiled, inherently perfected from the beginning.
Simply by leaving behind delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. At these words, his teacher attained awakening.

At the assembly for the parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One stroked his chest with his hand and addressed the multitude, saying: "You should all carefully contemplate my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold.
Gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied; do not let yourselves have cause for regret later. If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciples;
if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa, you likewise are not my disciples. At that time, the assembly of hundreds of billions of beings was entirely...
Regarding the realization of the Way, Yunfeng Yue said: "The gateway of the incurable is not sufficient to administer medicine.
Today, Yunfeng shall act as a physician for a dead horse. Do you people have blood under your skin?"
Yunmen asked Wulong, "Does one who has clarified their own nature still see a self? Wulong replied, "Only when one does not see a self does one begin to clarify it.
Yunmen asked again, "What is the level of realization for that which is learned on the long meditation couch?
Wulong said, "The second level. Yunmen asked, "What is the first level? Wulong said, "Tighten your straw sandals."
Miaoxi said: "Riding the bandit’s horse to pursue the bandit’s ranks; borrowing the old woman’s shawl to bow for New Year’s greetings.
Regarding the Chan Master Zheng of Zhongnan Mountain: because Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty was fond of eating clams, the officials along the coast grew weary of successively presenting them.
One day, there was one among the imperial kitchen staff that could not be pried open. The Emperor considered it a marvel and consequently burned incense to pray.
Upon opening it, he beheld the form of a Bodhisattva, fully endowed with the marks of a Brahmā.

The Emperor then placed it within a casket of gold-dusted sandalwood, covered it with fine brocade, and presented it for veneration by the monks of Xingshan Temple. He then asked his ministers, "What auspicious omen is this?

and consequently issued an edict to question the Master. The Master replied, "Your servant has heard that no phenomenon occurs without a corresponding cause. This is intended to awaken the Emperor’s faith."
[The Master] said, “I have heard. Thus, a sutra says: “For those who are to be delivered by this body, he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for them.
The Emperor said, “The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed appeared, yet we have not yet heard him preach the Dharma. The Master said, “Does Your Majesty regard this as permanent or impermanent?
Do you believe it or not? The Emperor said, “This is a rare and marvelous thing; I believe it deeply. The Master—
The Emperor said, "Your Majesty has already heard the teaching of the Dharma to its conclusion. His Imperial Majesty was greatly delighted, finding it something he had never experienced before.

He then issued an edict that every temple throughout the realm must establish an image of Avalokiteśvara. Master Shanzhao of Fenyang addressed the assembly, saying: "Every single phrase must embody the three mysteries; each mystery..."
The Gate must possess three essentials: illumination, function, and their relationship. There is illumination followed by function; there is function followed by illumination;
there is illumination and function simultaneously; and there is illumination and function at different times. As for illumination followed by function, I shall deliberate this with you.
As for function followed by illumination, you must be a person of substance before you can attain it. As for illumination and function simultaneously—how will you manage that?
When life arises, one should strike [the truth]. Illumination and function do not occur at the same time;
how then, you monk, will you find a way to settle into them? A monk asked, "What is the source of the Great Way? He replied, "Digging in the earth to seek the sky. "How can it be so?

"Because you do not recognize the profound mystery. The monk asked again, "What is the guest within the guest? He replied, "Joining palms before the hermitage to question the World-Honored One. The monk asked, "And what is the guest?"
[The Master] said: "Facing each other, there is no companion. [The Questioner] asked: "What is the guest within the host? [The Master] said: "Battle clouds stretch across the sea;
drawing the sword, he stirs the Dragon Gate. [The Questioner] asked: "What is the host within the host? [The Master] said:
"Three heads and six arms, upholding heaven and earth; the wrathful Nātha smashes the celestial bell."
Master Tong had read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* approximately one thousand times yet remained unable to comprehend the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*).
He went to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the three bodies:

the pure *dharmakāya* is your nature; the complete *saṃbhogakāya* is your wisdom; the hundreds of thousands of millions of *nirmāṇakāya* emanations are your practice. If you depart from your original nature..."

To speak of the three bodies (trikāya) is called having a body but lacking wisdom. If one awakens to the fact that the three bodies have no self-nature (niḥsvabhāva), this is called the Bodhi of the four wisdoms (caturjñāna).
Listen to my verse: The self-nature inherently possesses the three bodies; Its manifestation and illumination form the four wisdoms.

Without departing from the conditions of seeing and hearing, One transcends and ascends to the stage of Buddhahood. I now speak for you; believe it with certainty and forever be free from delusion. Do not emulate those who gallop in pursuit.

The seeker said, "I have heard you speak of Bodhi all day long; may I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms? The Patriarch replied, "Since you have already realized the three bodies, you must clearly understand the four wisdoms.
Why ask further? If one speaks of the four wisdoms apart from the three bodies, this is called having wisdom without a body.
Such 'wisdom' is in fact no wisdom at all. He then spoke a verse: "The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom..."
The Mirror-like Wisdom is pure in nature; the Wisdom of Equality has no affliction in its mind. The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees that there is no effort;

the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror. The five, eight, six, and seven [consciousnesses] transform as fruit and cause; they are merely conventional designations and lack any real intrinsic nature.

If one leaves no lingering attachment in the midst of activity, then amidst all proliferation, one forever dwells in the *nāga-samādhi*. [He] offered a general prostration of thanks and praised him with a verse:

"The three bodies are originally my own essence; The four wisdoms are fundamentally the luminosity of the mind. Body and wisdom merge without obstruction, Responding to things according to their forms.
To initiate cultivation is entirely deluded movement; To cling to a state is not true refinement. Through the Teacher, I have understood the wondrous principle, And shall never again be defiled."
[This is] the name [of the case]. Master Linji asked Longguang, "Without deploying a 'spiritual edge' (jīfēng), how can one achieve victory? Longguang sat firmly in his seat.
Linji said, "A great teacher of the Dharma—do you have no skillful means? Longguang then stared at him with wide eyes and said, "Ha! Linji pointed his finger [at him].
[Zhaozhou] said, "This old fellow has met with defeat today.
Miaoxi said, "It is a pity that Longguang let this fellow off.
Nevertheless, one must still rescue the old man Linji."
Master Baoning Yong addressed the assembly, saying: "Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly refrain from speaking.
To speak is for horns to grow. Great assembly, the horns have grown; now tell me, is it an ox or a horse? He further offered a verse on Yunmen’s "Mount Sumeru":
"Standing atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak is utterly wrong; In the blink of an eye, one falls over a precipice. The entire body is not damaged by a single hair."
As for "hair": how would one dare to bury it in heaven or among men?
Master Wuzu Yan addressed the assembly, saying: "To speak of Buddhas or speak of the Dharma, to wield the mallet or raise the whisk—ten thousand miles of white clouds."
Deshan would strike as soon as one entered the gate; Linji would shout as soon as one entered the gate. "White clouds ten thousand miles away.
After that, it is not permitted to act thus, nor is it permitted not to act thus; it is not permitted to do both thus and not thus—yet even so, it is "white clouds ten thousand miles away.
Suddenly, someone comes forth and says, "Venerable Sir, for you to speak in such a manner... Even so, it is "white clouds ten thousand miles away."
Li: "To speak in this way is called 'the dwarf watching a play, rising and falling along with the others. Thirty years from now, it will be a source of great laughter.
But tell me, what is there to laugh at? It is the laughter of 'ten thousand miles of white clouds. A monk asked, "The function is unobscured; I pray the Master will speak directly.
He replied, "Gathering them together and letting them go. He further addressed the assembly, saying: "Root and branch must return to the source; honor and humility..."
"Using his words: casting a sharp sword into the void; striking a rat with a great club.
While Yunyan was sweeping the floor, Daowu said, "Why do you trouble yourself so much? Yunyan replied, "You must know that there is one who does not trouble himself.
Daowu said, "If that is so, then there is a 'second moon'. Yunyan held up his broom and said, "This!"
"Which month is this? I shall now desist. Xuansha said, "Had I seen him at that time, I would have told him, 'This is precisely the second month.
Yunmen said, "The master is diligent toward his servant. Zhenru said, "Using diligence to compensate for clumsiness.
Among these three statements, one can settle the universe, one can test the monk, and one can [determine the standard].
This is to accommodate those of beginner capacity. Can you all still discern and distinguish this? If you can discern and distinguish it, I grant that you have personally seen the light of wisdom.
If you cannot discern it, do not say that the mountain ranges of the light of wisdom are steep and perilous; from afar across the river, one gazes upon the idleness of the green clouds.

Master Dongshan Chanshi addressed the assembly, saying: "To proclaim the lineage of the school and propagate the Great Teaching, one must possess a refined and keen Dharma-eye to be able to discern the black from the white.
This is because truth and falsehood share a single source; like water and milk in the same vessel, they are difficult to distinguish upon reaching this point.
Dongshan habitually observes external forms with the eye within the mind. Observing again and again, he then makes the distinction."
As for truth and falsehood: if it were not so, how could one be called a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend)?

Indeed, a *kalyāṇamitra* is one who drives away the oxen of the plowman and snatches the food from the hungry man; only then is one named a *kalyāṇamitra*. Among those in the world today, who is a true *kalyāṇamitra*?
O practitioners of Zen, you must consider how many such *kalyāṇamitras* you have encountered; this is no trivial matter. You must simply...
Investigate thoroughly and examine deeply until you penetrate through; even a thousand sages cannot verify it for you. Only then will the true man of great capacity be revealed.
Have you not seen how the Elder Śākyamuni attained sudden, great enlightenment when the morning star appeared, becoming a Buddha simultaneously with all sentient beings of the great earth?
There is no limit of before or after—how magnificent this is! Nevertheless, even so, were one to encounter a monk with clear eyes, he would also [say]:
"It would be better to strike his spine with a staff. A monk asked, "Vimalakīrti held up the four worlds in the palm of his hand; I wonder where Vimalakīrti’s own body was?
The Master said, "It is behind you, O teacher. The monk asked, "Why is it behind me? The Master said, "Give me back the head of the phrase.
He asked, "What is it like when there are no traces and not a single dot? The Master said, "A sharp peck-measure cannot exhaust it. He asked, "How is it? [The Master replied: "..."
This is the fundamental matter of the monk. It is said: "A camel crossing the Han River. He asked: "What is the one phrase that is truly intimate?
He replied: "Bodhidharma had no teeth in his front row."
When Deshan arrived at Guishan, he tucked up his outer robe and went straight up to the Dharma Hall. He walked from west to east and from east to west, looking around and saying, "Non-existent!
Non-existent! Then he departed. Reaching the entrance, he said again, "One must not be so hasty," and then entered with full ceremonial dignity to meet him.
While Guishan was seated, Deshan held up his sitting cloth and said, "Preceptor. Guishan—
As he was about to take up his whisk, Deshan gave a shout and swept out of the hall with his sleeves. Turning his back on the Dharma Hall, he put on his straw sandals and departed.
When Guishan returned in the evening, he asked the Head Seat, "Where has that newcomer gone?
The Head Seat replied, "He turned his back on the Dharma Hall, put on his straw sandals, and left. Guishan said, "In the future, this man will go to the summit of a solitary peak."
Panzhu built a grass hut, reviled the Buddhas, and cursed the patriarchs; he went away.
Miaoxi said, "When these two venerable masters met in this manner, each lost one of their eyes."
Miaoxi addressed the assembly, saying: "The ancients said: 'Great wisdom is without discrimination; great function is without principle or affairs.
It is like the moon reflecting in a thousand rivers, or like waves following the various waters. Now, what is this great wisdom that is without discrimination?
What is this great function that is without principle or affairs? Is it not the case that asking one and answering ten, with eloquence flowing like a cascading river, constitutes great wisdom?"
Is it not the case that "coarse words and subtle speech alike return to the primary meaning"?

Is it this kind of great function—such as overturning the meditation seat, shouting to disperse the assembly, striking the jaw with a palm, and sweeping the sleeves to depart, or instantly striking one across the mouth should they hesitate or deliberate?
If you hold such a view, do not even say "I am a patch-robed monk"; you would simply be one of those patch-robed monks.
Even a lowly servant who has discarded his straw sandals and carries a bag of antiques has not yet attained this.

A true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) may possess actual realization and verification, yet if they do not clarify the Great Dharma, when acting for others they cannot help but point toward their own state of self-realization and self-verification, thereby blinding the eyes of others.
How much more so for those who have neither realization nor verification and merely parrot the words—blinding the eyes of people is no small matter.
So it is said. This matter is extremely difficult. Even great beings of immeasurable capacity find no footing here;
how then can you petty-rooted, ignorant spawn of Māra dare to speak with such reckless audacity? Try sitting in a quiet place and examine this subtly:
has your inner mind truly reached the stage of non-doubt? If you have not truly reached it, [how can you speak so boldly]?
I, however, commend you for being able to let go and maintain composure, remaining unswayed by others. Those like you are called "dregs of hell.

Lay patrons from the ten directions bring you a grain of rice or a stalk of vegetable to provide for your needs, desiring only that your spiritual practice (*daoye*) be perfected so that you may together enter the Buddha Vehicle.
Yet you seek instead worldly blessings and rewards in future lives; thus, your spiritual practice remains unenlightened.
How can this be resolved? If you all truly desire to succeed to this lineage, you must ensure that mind and object are as one;

only then will there be a slight degree of correspondence. Do not, upon hearing me speak of such matters, simply close your eyes and hide your gaze, assuming a corpse-like posture and forcibly arranging for mind and object to be "as one. No matter what your skillful means may be, how could this ever suffice?

Arranging and aligning. Do you wish to truly attain the state where mind and environment are as one? You must break it completely, shatter it utterly, and cast away that which conjures delusive thoughts within the skull.
Cut a single stroke through the eighth consciousness, and naturally you will not be attached to such arrangements.
Have you not seen Master Yantou say: "As soon as there is something held as important, it becomes a conceptual trap"? You...
As for those people who have spent their entire lives in the monasteries seeking this matter and yet attained nothing, it goes without saying.
Among them, many have grown old with white hair and yellowed teeth, sitting within the confines of their habitual patterns, unable to emerge from them for their whole lives;
they do not recognize their own error. Those who derive some flavor from the words and phrases of the ancients take those extraordinary sayings and wondrous verses as their nest.
The Mortar. Those who find flavor in the sounds, names, phrases, and meanings within the scriptural teachings take those scriptures as their mortar.

Those who find flavor in the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients take the ancients’ questions and answers, their alternative expressions, their shifting tones, and their words of praise and censure as their mortar.
Those who find flavor in the nature of mind take the three realms as being... [only mind].
To take "the mind as the sole reality of all phenomena" (citta-mātra) as one's fundamental principle;

to find flavor in a state of silence, wordlessness, and ineffability, remaining motionless within a ghost cave beneath Black Mountain, with eyes closed and hidden beyond the era of Wei-yin—this is to take such a state as one's fundamental principle.

To find flavor in the midst of daily activities, movements, and functions—by raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, or lifting... [the hand]—this is to take such activity as one's fundamental principle.
To take awakening and alertness as one's habitual nest is to say that the Dharma does not reside in words and phrases,
nor in intellectual consciousness, nor in the sphere of physical movement and activity. To mistakenly identify karmic consciousness as Buddha-nature, and for those who find a "flavor" therein,
to take the spark struck from flint or a flash of lightning as their habitual nest— all such things as described above involve being attached to the place where one has found that flavor.
If one lacks the magnanimity of a great man and, upon retreating, recognizes one's error, yet immediately treats that which was previously valued as something extraordinary,
as something profound and mysterious, as something secure, as something ultimate, or as something liberating— those who form such conceptions [will fall].
Even the appearance of a Buddha in the world cannot change this. In the teachings, this is called the delusion of ignorant darkness (*moha-andhakāra*).
Why? Because due to your ignorance (*moha*), you grasp what is false as being true; because of your darkness, you fall into that which you value and are unable to move or turn away from it.
If there is nothing arising in the mind and no attachment to phenomena, then there will be nothing valued. When there is nothing valued, one naturally returns to the state of purity.
With the power of the bones, there is no desire and no dependence; one attains mastery over the Dharma. It is not difficult for you to achieve such resonance right now.
It simply requires that the mind be equanimous and free from any attachment. What constitutes attachment?

To form conceptions of sentient beings, conceptions of Buddhas, conceptions of the mundane world, conceptions of the supramundane, conceptions of seeking liberation, and conceptions of seeking Buddha-wisdom—all these are termed [attachment].
Regarding attachment: you need only exert your full vigor while desire is about to arise but has not yet arisen.
With a single leap, you will emerge; this mind will be luminous and uniquely liberated. As soon as you realize it is thus, you turn upward immediately.
Naturally, everything will be clear in every instance, and all things will manifest. Even when you reach such a state, you must not look back or cling to it. If you look back...
Where there is attachment, there is something held as weighty. As soon as there is something held as weighty, this mind immediately leaks away.
This is merely called a "leaking mind" and not a "mind of equality. What is called equality means that good and evil are equal; turning one's back and facing toward are equal;

principle and phenomena are equal; the ordinary and the sage are equal; the measurable and the immeasurable are equal; and essence and function are equal. This principle can only be realized through direct certification.
Only then will you know. If you have not yet realized it, you must realize it directly. Only upon realizing it can one be called a true child of the renunciant life.
If the mind does not realize it, yet seeks realization outside the mind, this is called an outsider among renunciants;

such a person is not even fit to be considered grass or weeds. This mind is vast and great, without measure or boundary; it is where the sands-of-the-Ganges Buddhas attain equal and perfect enlightenment.
Awakened awareness: the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe all do not transcend this mind.
This mind is able to bestow names and establish designations for all things, yet no thing can bestow a name or establish a designation for it.
Therefore, the Buddhas and Patriarchs, having no other choice, have followed along with your delusions and applied various names, calling it True Suchness, Buddha-nature, Bodhi, and Nirvana.
Various distinct and differing names are established because, within the realm of sentient beings, your views and understandings are biased and incomplete;
there are various differences, and thus these distinct names are established so that you may recognize this undifferentiated fundamental mind within the context of differentiation.
It is not that this mind itself possesses any differentiation. Therefore, when a monk asked Mazu, "How [is it]?"...
"This is Buddha. Zu said, "The mind itself is Buddha. If you have truly realized and awakened to this, what difference would there be?
If you do not awaken, yet seek a marvelous understanding, you will not truly realize or awaken; you will not believe that this very mind is definitively Buddha."
This very fact—that "this mind is itself Buddha"—is precisely the cause and condition for differentiation.
The Buddha said that he wished to demonstrate this through analogies, yet in the end, no analogy can truly illustrate it. To speak of it as "vast" already limits it;
how much more so to attempt to enter this vast realm with a limited mind? Even if one were to succeed in entering it, it would be like using a shell to scoop up the ocean.

Even if a single conch-shell were filled to the brim, how much could it actually contain? Yet, at the very moment you prevent the water from entering that shell, it is already an immeasurable amount of water.
Because your mental scope is limited to such a small extent, you conceive the thought of being fully satisfied.
Therefore, this immeasurable realm also appears to be filled according to the capacity of your own vessel; it is not that the great ocean itself is only that small a quantity.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "For example, the great ocean does not refuse even small streams; even mosquitoes, gadflies, and asuras who drink from its waters all obtain their fill.
This water is a metaphor for the mind; the mosquitoes, gadflies, and asuras are metaphors for the distinctions between large and small.
Within the essence of this mind, there are fundamentally no such various distinctions. You need only refrain from giving rise to various views and cognitions.
Grasp this mind; you shall personally recognize its various distinctions. Even the ancient sages did not permit the grasping of this mind as something real.
Aside from the mind, what other substantial entity exists to create obstacles for you?
My current muddling through is also unavoidable, for it is the "old woman’s heart" of one who, out of urgent compassion, seeks to guide her wayward child and cherish her beloved son.
Therefore, do not follow the branches and extend the vines; do not take what I say as being the final truth.
Today I speak thus, yet tomorrow I may speak otherwise. When you speak thus, I may speak otherwise; when you do not speak thus, I may speak thus.
Where would you go to seek my dwelling place? Even I myself do not know it.
As for this dwelling place, how can others ever find it? This is a living gateway; one must first see it while it is functioning before one can enter and practice.

Nowadays, students take a small measure of diligence—bowing to the Buddha, reciting scriptures, and maintaining the precepts of body, speech, and mind—as their provisions, hoping thereby to realize the goal.
What possible connection could there be? It is much like a fool burying his head.
One walks toward the west, yet wishes to take an object from the east; the further one turns and runs, the more one turns away, becoming increasingly urgent and increasingly slow.

This is the great Dharma-gate that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), untainted (*anāsrava*), and effortless (*anābhoga*). If even the slightest thought of seeking realization arises, one will immediately turn away from it.
How can you hope to achieve anything by relying on some minor conditioned practice? Therefore, the ancients saw [the truth] too clearly.
Because we are close at hand, I say, "I sit on the ground while you investigate," and I also say, "I stand on the ground while you investigate.
This does not mean that I am teaching you to create patterns or imitate forms, accumulating merit and virtue in hopes of attaining the Way.

Even if you were to attain it through such hope, as soon as it is attained, it would immediately perish; it would merely lead to self-exhaustion. Do not, upon hearing this, dismiss it as non-existent.
To create the karma of hell while claiming that one’s ordinary, uneventful state is the "absence of Buddhist dharma-knowledge and vision"—
to simply eat when hungry and sleep when tired, taking this to be "no cultivation or realization" and "no effort"—
do not misunderstand this! To shoulder this matter, one must be a person forged from solid steel and cast from raw iron.
Han [Shi] has only just begun to attain it. How could you, with such meager roots and limited capacity, presume to receive and uphold it so hastily?
Have you not seen how Linji questioned Huangbo three times about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma and was beaten each time?
Only later, upon being pointed out by Dayu, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. Unconsciously letting out a cry, he said, "Aha! So, Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much after all. Dayu said:

Children and grandchildren, you truly do not disgrace me. Since ancient times, there has fortunately been such a standard;

This kind of expression is called the "Mystery within the Phrase" (zhongzhong xuan). It is the phrase that cuts off all streams: like treading upon the beam of a scale, hard as iron;

like walking only when walking and sitting only when sitting; like the large month having thirty days and the small month having twenty-nine. Bring this forth!
This kind of category is called "the mystery within mysteries" (xuánzhōng xuán). It is a phrase that follows the waves and pursues the currents. Have you not seen how Master Fenyang’s verse says:
"The three mysteries and three essentials are difficult to distinguish; When one attains the meaning, one forgets the words, and the Way becomes easy to approach.
A single phrase, luminously clear, encompasses the myriad phenomena; On the Double-Ninth Festival, the chrysanthemums are fresh. This old man has clearly pointed this out for you.
The very marrow of Linji has been brought forth here to be annotated phrase by phrase. "The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish" is the general verse.

"When the meaning is grasped, words are forgotten; the Way is easy to approach" refers to the Mystery within the Essence (*ti-chung-hsüan*). "A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena" refers to the Mystery within the Phrase (*chü-chung-hsüan*).
"On the Double-Ninth Festival, the chrysanthemums are fresh" refers to the Mystery within the Mystery (*hsüan-chung-hsüan*). This is [the teaching] of the former masters.
Though he bears a great reputation and claims to have attained true awakening, he lacks clarity regarding the Great Dharma;

He told you clearly: "The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; when one attains the meaning, one forgets the words."
It is said that the Way is easy to approach. A single phrase, clearly manifest, encompasses the myriad phenomena: on the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh.

Buried. Lest it lead to the corruption of the men and women of others' families. "One blind man leading a multitude of blind men. When questioned regarding the Three Essentials, one cannot provide an explanatory commentary.

Taking two parts white and one part black as a circle represents "centered within the biased. Thus, one comes to speak of the white from the perspective of the dark, yet without transgressing against the white itself.

The Path. Regarding affairs on the periphery of humanity, one is also able to employ "reciprocal interfusion" (*huìhù*). The subtlety lies in embodying what precedes. This is called "reaching within the simultaneous":

It is precisely without partiality; therefore, it is called the "Vast and Mysterious Essential Path" and the "Unattached True Doctrine. The former masters of old have deduced that this single stage is the most wondrous and the most profound.

This means that this matter cannot be without merit or have interruptions even while one is eating a meal. "What is it like when one is serving [it]?"

"At that time, what is it like? This means that the Dharma and the object are in opposition. The answer is: "One does not obtain form. This means that the Dharma and the object cannot become a single form.

Each of you should take advantage of your current vigor and strength, exerting your spirit to realize it for yourselves. Do not crave what is "extraordinary," for such extraordinariness deceives and misleads people, leaving a mixture of poison within the consciousness.

Nor does it borrow the vital power from others; this is a matter each person possesses fully within their own domain.

Simply do not harbor likes or dislikes; let it be transparently clear. A difference as slight as a hair’s breadth makes worlds apart.

If you wish to see what is before you, do not maintain notions of compliance or resistance. Every one of you monks can recite this, but have you ever applied even a fraction of your mind to understand its meaning?

The Patriarch bestowed upon it the name "Inscription on Faith" (*Xinxin Ming*). Its sole purpose is to lead all people to have faith in this vast, quiescent, and wondrous mind, which is definitively not obtained from others.
Thus, within the text it says: "When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
